title: Ezekiel Uses Sexual Imagery So Graphic Many Churches Skip the Chapter
paragraphs: Ezekiel Uses Sexual Imagery So Graphic Many Churches Skip the Chapter
The Bible does not sanitize spiritual adultery. Ezekiel makes it disturbing on purpose—and buried beneath the shame is one of Scripture’s most breathtaking movements from scandal to grace.
There are chapters of the Bible people underline.
There are chapters they turn into wall art.
There are chapters preached at weddings, funerals, conferences, and Sunday services.
And then there is Ezekiel 16.
A chapter so uncomfortable that reading portions of it aloud can make an entire room suddenly interested in the floor.
And Ezekiel 23 goes further still.
The language becomes sexual. Graphic. Humiliating. At points, shocking enough that modern readers may wonder why words like these are even in Holy Scripture.
But perhaps the more dangerous question is not, “Why would God allow language this disturbing in the Bible?”
Perhaps it is...
What was happening in the human heart that required language this disturbing to expose it?
Because Ezekiel was not writing pornography.
He was prosecuting idolatry.
And when you understand what God was exposing, the chapter stops being merely about ancient Jerusalem.
It starts reading your heart.
That is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Jerusalem had been loved.
Chosen.
Covered.
Adorned.
Provided for.
Yet she took the very gifts God had given her and used them in spiritual unfaithfulness.
Ezekiel describes Jerusalem metaphorically as a woman whom God rescued, cared for, entered into covenant with, clothed, adorned, and established. Then comes the devastating turn.
The Hebrew of Ezekiel 16:15 says:
וַתִּבְטְחִי בְיָפְיֵךְ ... וַתִּזְנִי
Vattivtechi veyofyekh ... vattizni.
In context:
“But you trusted in your beauty ... and prostituted yourself.”
That final Hebrew verb comes from the root זנה — zanah, a word associated with prostitution or sexual unfaithfulness.
That matters.
God could have described Israel merely as “disobedient.”
He could have said they had “made poor choices.”
He could have softened it into the kind of religious vocabulary that allows people to feel convicted for eleven minutes and then go home unchanged.
He did not.
Through Ezekiel, covenant betrayal is portrayed as adultery.
Why?
Because idolatry is not merely breaking a regulation.
It is betraying a relationship.
That changes everything.
Imagine a husband discovering that the person to whom he gave his heart has been secretly giving herself to someone else.
Imagine the photographs.
The messages.
The lies.
The realization that some of the gifts he bought her were worn while she went to meet another man.
Now imagine someone walking into the room and saying:
“Relax. She merely violated a technical requirement of the marriage contract.”
You would know immediately how absurd that sounds.
Because betrayal is personal.
And that is precisely what respectable religion sometimes allows us to forget about sin.
We reduce sin to rule-breaking.
God reveals it as rebellion against the One who loved us.
We call it a habit.
God sees what it worships.
We call it a private struggle.
God sees what it is doing to our soul.
We call it “just entertainment.”
“Just flirting.”
“Just bitterness.”
“Just ambition.”
“Just another purchase.”
“Just one more drink.”
“Just another fantasy.”
“Just the way I am.”
“Just something nobody knows about.”
But Ezekiel tears the word just away.
Jerusalem's tragedy was not merely that she sinned.
She received gifts from God and then used those gifts apart from God.
And that possibility has not disappeared.
The body God gave you can become an instrument of lust.
The mind God gave you can become consumed by pride.
The money God entrusted to you can become your security.
The career God allowed you to build can become your identity.
The influence God permitted you to have can become an altar where you worship applause.
Even ministry can become something we secretly use to make people notice us instead of Jesus.
That is when Ezekiel gets frighteningly close.
Because idols are not always statues.
Sometimes they have screens.
Sometimes they have bank accounts.
Sometimes they have follower counts.
Sometimes they have another person's face.
Sometimes the idol looking back at us from the mirror is ourselves.
And sometimes the most dangerous idols are good things that quietly inherited the place belonging only to God.
Ezekiel refuses to make this pretty.
In chapter 23, he portrays Samaria and Jerusalem through two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, whose sexual promiscuity symbolizes their idolatry and their faithless pursuit of foreign powers.
Then Ezekiel 23:20 uses imagery so explicit that its force survives even across thousands of years.
The Hebrew reads:
אֲשֶׁר בְּשַׂר חֲמוֹרִים בְּשָׂרָם וְזִרְמַת סוּסִים זִרְמָתָם
A close rendering is:
“whose flesh was like the flesh of donkeys, and whose emission was like that of horses.”
Yes.
That is in the Bible.
And no, its presence does not mean Scripture is celebrating sexual depravity.
The opposite is happening.
The imagery is intentionally degrading because Ezekiel is exposing the degrading insanity of Jerusalem's lust after other nations, their power, and their gods.
The prophetic metaphor is supposed to repel you.
It is judgment language.
It is not seduction.
That distinction is essential.

Scripture sometimes describes evil vividly without endorsing evil. A surgeon can expose a wound because he intends to heal it. A prophet can expose corruption because polite language might allow the people to continue pretending nothing is wrong.
Ezekiel is holding up the wound.
And we want him to put it away.
Because somewhere inside us, we recognize it.
Maybe your idol has never been carved from wood.
Maybe nobody at church knows its name.
Maybe you know exactly when you usually return to it.
Late at night.
When the marriage feels empty.
When anxiety gets loud.
When loneliness arrives.
When somebody hurts you.
When you feel invisible.
When God seems silent.
You reach for something.
A person.
Pornography.
Food.
Alcohol.
Money.
Work.
Attention.
Fantasy.
Anger.
Control.
Validation.
A secret relationship.
Endless scrolling.
Anything capable of making you feel different for a few minutes.
And underneath the behavior is often a deeper spiritual question:
Where do I run when I do not believe God will be enough for me here?
That question can expose an altar.
This is why Ezekiel's sexual imagery should not merely make us blush.
It should make us examine ourselves.
Because the terrifying part of spiritual adultery is that you can continue speaking God's name while your heart is sleeping with another master.
You can sing worship songs and worship approval.
You can quote Scripture and worship control.
You can preach surrender and worship reputation.
You can publicly say, “Jesus is Lord,” while privately organizing your life around something you are terrified to lose.
Jesus Himself later said:
“For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
The Gospel does not merely ask what your mouth calls God.
It reaches for the throne of your heart.
And here is where Ezekiel 16 becomes almost unbearable.
Because Jerusalem was not simply unfaithful.
She was unfaithful after being loved.
That is the scandal.
God had shown covenant kindness, and she responded with betrayal.
And if the chapter ended only with exposure and judgment, it would already be terrifying.
But it does not end there.
This is where grace enters the wreckage.
After pages of accusation, shame, judgment, and covenant infidelity, God says something astonishing.
Ezekiel 16:60:
וְזָכַרְתִּי אֲנִי אֶת־בְּרִיתִי אוֹתָךְ בִּימֵי נְעוּרָיִךְ וַהֲקִמוֹתִי לָךְ בְּרִית עוֹלָם
A close translation is:
“Yet I will remember my covenant with you in the days of your youth, and I will establish for you an everlasting covenant.”
Read that again.
Not because Jerusalem deserved another chance.
Not because the betrayal was insignificant.
Not because God suddenly decided sin did not matter.
Grace appears while the ugliness of the scandal is still visible.
“I will remember...”
The betrayed God speaks of covenant mercy.
That is not cheap grace.
Cheap grace says sin was never that serious.
Biblical grace says sin was so serious that reconciliation required an act of God.

And for Christians reading Ezekiel within the whole story of Scripture, that promise of covenant restoration belongs to the great biblical movement that reaches toward the new covenant and finds its fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
Ezekiel later speaks of cleansing, a new heart, and a new spirit.
Then, centuries later, on the night He was betrayed, Jesus lifted the cup and spoke of “the new covenant in my blood.”
Think about the irony.
Human beings became covenant breakers.
Jesus remained faithful.
We wandered.
He came looking for sinners.
We accumulated shame.
He carried shame to a Roman cross.
We deserved judgment.
He bore judgment for sinners.
We could not scrub ourselves clean enough to return home.
So Christ did not wait at a distance shouting instructions about how filthy people could climb back to God.
He came to save.
The cross is where Christianity destroys both arrogance and despair.
Arrogance dies because your sin is serious enough that the Son of God had to die.
Despair dies because the Son of God loved sinners enough to die.
That is the Gospel.
Not “try harder.”
Not “hide better.”
Not “make sure church people never discover what happened.”
Not “clean yourself up until Jesus can tolerate you.”
Repent.
Turn from sin.
Come to Christ.
Trust the crucified and risen Savior.
Receive the mercy you cannot manufacture.
And then follow Him.
This does not mean repentance is optional.
Grace never turns adultery into faithfulness by renaming adultery.
Jesus does not save us so that we can comfortably remain enslaved to the idols destroying us.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He calls.
He transforms.
The same Christ who says, “Come,” also says, “Follow Me.”
Maybe that is the sentence someone reading this fears most.
Because following Jesus may mean walking away from the thing you have been using to survive without Him.
Deleting the number.
Ending the affair.
Confessing the addiction.
Giving up the hidden account.
Returning what was stolen.
Apologizing without defending yourself.
Getting accountable.
Forgiving someone whose name still makes your chest tighten.
Admitting that your “ambition” became worship.
Admitting that your “relationship” became an idol.
Admitting that what you called freedom has actually been owning you.
Repentance can feel like death because something does die.
The illusion that we can keep our idols and still possess Jesus on our own terms.
But on the other side of surrender is something your idol could never give you.
Freedom.
The idol always makes promises before it takes payment.
Jesus tells you the cost and then gives you life.
The idol says, “Hide.”
Jesus brings you into the light.
The idol says, “You need me.”
Jesus says, “Come to Me.”
The idol feeds on your shame.
Jesus bore shame.
The idol demands more and gives less.
Christ gave Himself.
Perhaps you have spent years believing the most important fact about you is the worst thing you ever did.
It isn't.
If you belong to Christ, your scandal does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
This does not erase consequences.
It does not make victims irrelevant.
It does not call evil good.
Biblical forgiveness never requires us to pretend wounds were imaginary.
Grace is more powerful than denial precisely because grace looks directly at sin and still announces that redemption is possible through Christ.
Peter denied Jesus.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The Corinthian church contained people coming out of profound sexual and moral brokenness.
Yet the New Testament does not present redemption as God discovering unusually clean people.
It presents redemption as God saving sinners.
That means your past may explain your scars without being permitted to become your god.
You may have committed sexual sin.
You may have betrayed somebody.
You may have been betrayed.
You may have destroyed trust.
You may have spent years addicted to something you swore you could stop tomorrow.
You may have a secret that would change the way some people look at you.
You may have walked so far from God that reading an article about repentance feels almost insulting because you assume someone like you is beyond returning.
Listen carefully.
Ezekiel's message does not give you permission to minimize sin.
The Gospel gives you something infinitely better.
Permission to stop hiding and come to Jesus.
There is a difference between condemnation that drives you away from God and conviction that drives you toward repentance and mercy.
The enemy would love for you to read a chapter like Ezekiel 16 and conclude:
“Filthy. Finished. Unwanted.”
But the chapter itself moves toward covenant mercy.
And the Christian Gospel goes further still by showing us the price of that mercy.
A cross.
Blood.
A Savior.
An empty tomb.
Jesus Christ did not rise from the dead so that forgiven sinners could spend the rest of their lives introducing themselves by the name of their chains.
There is another name available.
Redeemed.
Not innocent because you never sinned.
Redeemed because Christ saves sinners.
That is why the Gospel is scandalous.
God does not merely renovate respectable people.
He raises the spiritually dead.
He receives repentant prodigals.
He forgives the guilty.
He cleanses the defiled.
He breaks chains.
He gives new hearts.
He takes stories we would have hidden forever and turns them into testimonies that make other wounded people believe there might still be hope for them too.
Not because scandal does not matter.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And maybe now you understand why Ezekiel had to be so graphic.
Sometimes we need language strong enough to destroy our ability to romanticize what is killing us.
Sometimes the wound must be uncovered before we will ask for healing.
Sometimes God allows the mirror to become painfully clear because mercy is standing behind us, waiting for us to stop pretending.
So do not merely ask, “How could Israel do this?”
Ask:
Where have I done this?
What gift from God became more important than God?
What do I run toward before I run toward Jesus?
What am I protecting that Christ is asking me to surrender?
What secret keeps demanding darkness?
What would obedience cost me today?
And what would continuing in rebellion eventually cost me?
Do not answer publicly because somebody pressured you.
But do answer God truthfully.
And if this exposed something you have kept hidden, you do not need to tell strangers every detail.
Your comment may become the sentence another ashamed believer needed to see tonight.
Your testimony may remind somebody that repentance is not the funeral of hope.
It is the road home.
And if one person's face came into your mind while reading this, do not ignore it.
Better yet, send this privately when the struggle is sensitive.
It does not.
It is not.
We glorify God through faith in Christ and lives of worship, obedience, love, generosity, truth, and faithful stewardship.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical expression of generosity when you believe that work is faithfully helping people encounter Scripture and hear about Jesus.
Jesus is calling sinners to Himself.
You cannot buy that invitation.
You cannot merchandise your way into it.
You cannot earn it by sharing a Christian post.
Salvation is not for sale.
Christ paid the price.
Your response is repentance and faith.
So share because someone needs truth.
Tag because somebody you love may need reminding that God has not abandoned them.
Save because you may need these words again.
Follow because staying near Scripture matters in a world discipling your attention every hour.
Support Gospel work if God has given you the desire and means to do so.
But above everything...
Follow Jesus.
Because one day the likes disappear.
The algorithms stop mattering.
The merchandise wears out.
The platforms vanish.
Our earthly names are forgotten.
But Christ remains.
And perhaps the most shocking thing about Ezekiel's disturbing portrait of unfaithfulness is not how far God's people wandered.
It is that after exposing the betrayal, God still spoke of covenant mercy.
That is the line you should carry with you when you close this article.
When Satan tells you your scandal is too filthy for grace, remember the cross proves that Jesus already knew the depth of human sin—and came for sinners anyway.
Your darkest chapter may tell the truth about where you have been, but only Jesus has the authority to write the final sentence.
